seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 92 HTS Chapter 17 lines — raw and refined cane and beet sugar, maple syrup, glucose and fructose syrups, lactose, molasses, candy and chewing gum. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, the sugar tariff-rate quotas, the 2026 Section 301 duties and the Canada Section 338 duties.

overview.intro:
Chapter 17 covers sugars and sugar confectionery: raw and refined cane and beet sugar, maple syrup, glucose, fructose and lactose, molasses, and candy and chewing gum without cocoa. Its **92 tariff lines** are built around the **U.S. sugar quotas**. Raw cane sugar entered with a certificate of quota eligibility pays about **1.4¢/kg** (scaled by polarity) and refined sugar about 3.7¢/kg; **above the quota the same sugar pays 33.87¢ or 35.74¢ per kg** — often more than the sugar is worth. Candy pays 4% to 12.2%.

The U.S. imported **$6.48B** of Chapter 17 goods in 2025: candy $3.31B (Mexico $1.24B, Canada $650M), raw cane sugar $1.29B and maple syrup $387M. In-quota raw and refined sugar is **exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties**; everything else from the 60 Section 301 economies pays them since **July 24, 2026** — 10% in total for EU candy, +12.5% for Türkiye, Thailand, Colombia and Australia, +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying Mexican and Canadian goods enter free — including **Canadian maple syrup** — but Canadian lactose, glucose syrups and molasses pay 50% under Section 338, and Canadian molasses is banned from September 29, 2026.

productGroups.label: Cane or beet sugar and chemically pure sucrose (raw and refined)
productGroups.blurb: Raw cane sugar entered under a country's quota allocation (with a certificate of quota eligibility) pays 1.4606¢/kg less 0.020668¢ per degree under 100° polarity — about 1.38¢/kg at 96°; refined sugar in quota 3.6606¢/kg. Above quota: 33.87¢/kg raw, 35.74¢/kg refined. In-quota sugar is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. Mexico ($531M) supplies under the suspension agreements; the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Colombia and El Salvador under their quotas.
productGroups.rateSummary: ≈1.4¢/kg raw · ≈3.7¢/kg refined in quota · 33.87¢/kg · 35.74¢/kg over quota

productGroups.label: Other sugars and syrups: maple syrup, glucose, fructose, lactose, invert sugar
productGroups.blurb: Maple syrup and maple sugar are Free (Canada, $387M); glucose syrup 2.2¢/kg, fructose 5.1%, lactose 6.4%. Sugar syrups and blends with cane or beet sugar fall under the sugar quotas: 6% in quota, 16.9¢–33.9¢/kg of total sugars + 5.1% over quota. Canadian lactose, glucose and fructose syrups pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Molasses
productGroups.blurb: Cane and beet molasses pay 0.35¢/liter for sugar extraction or feed, otherwise 0.01¢/kg of total sugars. Central America supplies most. Canadian molasses is banned from September 29, 2026.

productGroups.label: Sugar confectionery without cocoa (candy, gum, white chocolate)
productGroups.blurb: The largest group: $3.31B in 2025, $1.24B of it from Mexico and $650M from Canada. Hard and gummy candy pays 5.6%, chewing gum 4%, candied nuts 4.5%, cough drops Free; candy with over 10% or 65% sugar for further processing falls under quotas (12.2% in quota, 40¢/kg + 10.4% over). EU candy pays 10% in total since July 24, 2026.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** Not covered: sugar confectionery containing cocoa (1806); chemically pure sugars other than sucrose, lactose, maltose, glucose and fructose (2940); medicaments (chapter 30).

**Subheading note 1.** "Raw sugar" (1701.12–1701.14) has a sucrose content, in the dry state, corresponding to a polarimeter reading below 99.5°.

**Subheading note 2.** 1701.13 covers only non-centrifugal cane sugar (such as panela) polarizing 69° or more but less than 93°, with natural microcrystals surrounded by molasses residues.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**Note 1.** "Degree" in the rate columns means sugar degree by polarimetric test — the in-quota sugar rates fall by 0.020668¢/kg for each degree under 100°.

**Notes 2–4.** Define "articles containing over 65%" and "over 10%" of cane or beet sugar, and "blended syrups", that are capable of further processing and not packed for the retail consumer — the sugar-containing products under quota.

**Note 5.** The raw cane sugar quota (1701.13.10, 1701.14.10) is set each fiscal year by the Secretary of Agriculture at no less than 1,117,195 metric tons raw value, and the quota for refined and other sugars, syrups and molasses (1701.12.10, 1701.91.10, 1701.99.10, 1702.90.10, 2106.90.44) at no less than 22,000 t; USTR allocates them among countries and may require certificates of eligibility. Raw value is computed at 96° polarity.

**Note 6.** Raw cane sugar under 1701.13.20 and 1701.14.20 may be entered only for making polyhydric alcohols, or to be refined and re-exported (or substituted for exported domestic sugar), under USDA license.

**Notes 7–9.** The in-quota quantity is none for over-65% sugar articles (note 7) and blended syrups (note 9); 64,709 t a year for over-10% sugar-containing products (note 8), with Mexico excluded.

**Note 10.** Heading 1703 excludes products with 6% or less soluble non-sugar solids.

**Note 11.** "Cough drops" (1704.90.25) contain at least 5 mg of menthol or eucalyptol per dose.

seo.title: HTS Chapter 17 Sugar & Candy Tariff Updates — FY2027 Sugar Quotas, Section 301, Canada | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for sugar, syrup and candy imports (HTS Chapter 17) since January 2025: the FY 2027 sugar quota allocations, the in-quota sugar exemption from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, the Canada Section 338 duties and molasses ban, the Mexico sugar agreements and the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 17 base rate changed**: 90 of 92 lines are identical and the other 2 are a new certified-organic split of 1702.90.90 at the same 5.1%. The sugar quotas were reset for **FY 2027** (October 1, 2026): 1,117,195 t raw value of raw cane sugar and 22,000 t of refined sugar.

The changes came on top. The 2025 IEEPA duties ended on **February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** goods of 60 economies pay a Section 301 duty, but **in-quota raw and refined sugar is exempt**; candy, syrups and over-quota sugar are not — 10% in total for EU goods, +12.5% for Türkiye, Thailand, Colombia, Australia and the Dominican Republic, +37.5% for Brazil. **Canada** pays 50% under Section 338 on lactose, glucose and fructose syrups and molasses since August 22, 2026, and Canadian molasses is banned from September 29, 2026. Maple syrup is not affected.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 17 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies with the in-quota sugar exemption, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the older China Section 301 lists, the Canada Section 338 duties and import ban, the Nicaragua Section 301 tariff that starts in 2027, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, the yearly sugar quota allocations, and the suspension agreements on sugar from Mexico. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 17 base-rate changes
changes.detail: 90 of 92 lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; none changed. Two lines are a new certified-organic split of other sugars and syrups (1702.90.90.20/.50) at 5.1%.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 duty: 10% from 2027, 15% from 2028
changes.detail: USTR set a phased duty on products of Nicaragua (9903.89.01): 0% in 2026, 10% from January 1, 2027 and 15% from January 1, 2028. It does not apply to goods that originate under CAFTA-DR (U.S. note 29), such as Nicaraguan sugar and molasses entered with a CAFTA-DR claim.

changes.title: Canadian molasses banned from import
changes.detail: Proclamation 11062 excludes from importation, for goods imported from 12:01 a.m. ET on September 29, 2026, Canadian invert molasses (1702.90.35) and cane and beet molasses (1703.10.30, 1703.10.50, 1703.90.30, 1703.90.50), which had paid the 50% Section 338 dairy duty since August 22.

changes.title: FY 2027 raw sugar quota fully allocated
changes.detail: USTR allocated the remaining 55,993 t raw value of the FY 2027 raw cane sugar quota among 28 countries (for example Dominican Republic +11,931 t, Philippines +9,151 t, Australia +5,626 t). In-quota sugar may enter from October 1, 2026 with a certificate of quota eligibility.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 dairy duty reaches lactose, syrups and molasses
changes.detail: Proclamation 11047 (dairy) put 50% on 12 Chapter 17 lines of Canadian goods (9903.03.13): lactose, over-quota glucose, fructose and sugar syrups, invert molasses and molasses. Set for August 19, it was suspended for three days (Proclamation 11056) and took effect on August 22, 2026, and it applies even with a USMCA claim. Maple syrup, candy and sugar are not on the list.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies — in-quota sugar exempt
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), except the six in-quota sugar and syrup lines of additional U.S. note 5 (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). EU goods pay 10% in total when the base rate is lower. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). Candy, syrups and over-quota sugar pay the duty.

changes.title: FY 2027 sugar quota allocations by country
changes.detail: USTR allocated 1,061,202 t raw value of raw cane sugar among 39 countries — largest the Dominican Republic (189,343 t), the Philippines (145,235 t), Brazil (100,000 t) and Australia (89,293 t) — and the 22,000 t refined sugar quota: 10,300 t to Canada, 2,954 t to Mexico, 7,090 t first come first served, plus 1,656 t of specialty sugar. Of the 64,709 t sugar-containing products quota, 59,250 t went to Canada.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), with no Chapter 17 line exempt — in-quota Brazilian sugar pays it too. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) stacks on top for everything except in-quota sugar.

changes.title: FY 2027 sugar quotas set at the WTO minimum
changes.detail: USDA set the FY 2027 (October 1, 2026 – September 30, 2027) raw cane sugar quota at 1,117,195 metric tons raw value and the refined sugar quota at 22,000 t — the minimum U.S. WTO commitments.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims still keep Mexican and Canadian candy, sugar and maple syrup duty-free.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Mexico sugar suspension agreements continued
changes.detail: After five-year (sunset) reviews, Commerce continued the agreements suspending the antidumping and countervailing duty investigations on sugar from Mexico. They cap how much Mexican sugar may be exported to the United States and set minimum prices; USMCA keeps Mexican sugar duty-free within them.

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country rates, for example Thailand +19%, Türkiye +15%, and EU goods 15% in total including the base rate. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 40% IEEPA duty on products of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 (signed July 30, 2025) added 40% on goods of Brazil from August 6, 2025, on top of the 10% reciprocal duty. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). USMCA-qualifying goods stayed exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025 on Chapter 17 goods except those of Canada and Mexico; country rates followed on August 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 17 goods fell from **$7.17B in 2024 to $6.48B in 2025** (−9.7%), the first drop since 2020 ($4.91B). The fall is almost all **raw cane sugar**: 1701.14 dropped from $1.93B to $1.29B (−33%), and imports from **Brazil** from $880M to $316M (−64%). Beyond its quota allocation, Brazilian sugar pays the over-quota rate of 33.87¢/kg, and in 2025 it also paid the 10% reciprocal duty from April 5 and an extra 40% from August 6 — no Chapter 17 line was on either exemption list. Molasses fell 34%.

Candy held steady at $3.31B — Mexico ($1.24B) and Canada ($650M) ship it duty-free under USMCA — and maple syrup rose 15% to $387M. Mexico (+5.6%, $1.92B) and Canada (+7.7%, $1.18B) together supplied 48% of the chapter. Türkiye grew 12.9% to $232M, mostly candy.

Sugar volumes are set by policy as much as by markets: the yearly WTO quotas (1,117,195 t of raw cane sugar for FY 2027) and the agreements limiting Mexican sugar decide how much enters at the low rate. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data, so the 2026 Section 301 and Canada Section 338 duties are not yet visible in these figures.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on sugar depends on **whether it enters in quota** as much as on the country; for syrups and candy it depends on the country. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — computed from the current tariff schedule with the same engine as the tariff calculator.

**In-quota sugar pays no Section 301 duty**, and with a CAFTA-DR or Colombia claim no duty at all. Over-quota sugar pays 33.87¢–35.74¢/kg plus the country's extra duty. Candy and syrups pay the base rate plus **10% in total for the EU**, +10% or +12.5% for most countries, **+37.5% for Brazil** and +20% or +37.5% for China. **USMCA-qualifying Mexican and Canadian goods enter free**, except that Canadian lactose, glucose syrups and molasses pay 50% under Section 338, and Canadian molasses is banned.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-12, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; CAFTA-DR (P) for Guatemala, El Salvador and the Dominican Republic; CO for Colombia; AU for Australia. GSP (A, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020 and is not applied. An FTA claim removes the base rate but not the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)), and for Canada it does not remove the Section 338 duty (U.S. note 51(a)).
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.

In quota vs. over quota: the sugar group mixes in-quota lines (a low polarity-scaled rate, needing the country's allocation and a certificate of quota eligibility) and over-quota "Other" lines at 33.87¢–35.74¢/kg. The in-quota raw sugar rate is shown as "1.4606¢/kg (polarity-scaled)": 1.4606¢/kg less 0.020668¢/kg for each degree under 100° polarity, at least 0.943854¢/kg (about 1.38¢/kg at 96°); refined sugar starts from 3.6606¢/kg. Select a cell to see the lines.
Mexican sugar is duty-free under USMCA but the volume Mexico may export is limited by the suspension agreements; the matrix shows the tariff only.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 17: Sugars and Sugar Confectionery — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Sugar & Candy into the U.S.: Quota Certificates, Re-Export Program, FDA Rules & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 17) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The documents and rules for each HTS Chapter 17 line — certificates of quota eligibility for sugar, the USDA sugar re-export and polyhydric alcohol programs, the Mexico sugar agreements, FDA prior notice and supplier verification — and the legal ways to pay less: in-quota entry, USMCA and FTA claims, Chapter 98, drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For sugar the first question is **whether it enters in quota**: raw and refined sugar pays the low rate only against a country's allocation, with a **certificate of quota eligibility** issued by the exporting country, or under a **USDA re-export or polyhydric alcohol license**; otherwise it pays 33.87¢–35.74¢/kg. Mexican sugar enters under USMCA within the limits of the suspension agreements. Candy, syrups and other sugars are ordinary FDA foods: prior notice for every shipment and a foreign supplier verification program for the importer.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: **enter in quota**, use the **re-export program**, **claim USMCA or an FTA**, use **Chapter 98** for returned goods, or claim **drawback**. Each depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Enter sugar in quota with a certificate of quota eligibility
levers.saves: The difference between about 1.38¢/kg and 33.87¢/kg on raw sugar — about $3.25M on 10,000 t — and, for Section 301 economies, the 10%–12.5% extra duty
levers.appliesTo: Raw cane sugar (1701.13.10, 1701.14.10) and refined sugar and syrups (1701.12.10, 1701.91.10, 1701.99.10, 1702.90.10) within the country's fiscal-year allocation
levers.document: A certificate of quota eligibility issued by the exporting country's government for the allocation, presented at entry. FY 2027 allocations run from October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027.
levers.caveat: Only countries with an allocation (or the first-come, first-served refined sugar quantity) qualify; once an allocation is used, the over-quota rate applies.

levers.title: Use the USDA sugar re-export or polyhydric alcohol program
levers.saves: Raw sugar entered under 1701.13.20 / 1701.14.20 pays the low polarity-scaled rate outside the quota limits
levers.appliesTo: Raw cane sugar to be refined and re-exported (as sugar or in sugar-containing products) or used to make polyhydric alcohols
levers.document: A USDA license under the refined sugar re-export, sugar-containing products re-export or polyhydric alcohol program, with the export or use records it requires.
levers.caveat: The sugar must be used only for the licensed purpose (additional U.S. note 6); USDA can impose penalties for diversion.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on candy, syrups and sugar from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 35.74¢/kg on sugar) and the 10% Section 301 duty
levers.appliesTo: All 92 lines for qualifying Mexican goods; Canadian goods on lines whose Special column lists S, or within Canada's USMCA quantities
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, on the invoice or another document; CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Mexican sugar must also be covered by the export limits of the suspension agreements. For Canada the 50% Section 338 duty on lactose, syrups and molasses applies even with USMCA (U.S. note 51(a)). The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: Sugar from Mexico: suspension agreements continued (90 FR 45182)

levers.title: Claim CAFTA-DR, Colombia, Peru, Australia or another FTA
levers.saves: The base rate — on in-quota sugar the whole duty; on candy and syrups the Section 301 duty stays
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose Special column lists the agreement; CAFTA-DR, Peru, Colombia and Panama also have their own extra sugar quantities in Chapter 98 (9822.05.15, 9822.05.20, 9822.06.10, 9822.08.01)
levers.document: A claim on the entry with the agreement's certification or origin information — for example CAFTA-DR (19 CFR 10.583) or Australia (19 CFR 10.703).
levers.caveat: An FTA claim does not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty outside the in-quota sugar lines (U.S. note 52(a)).

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the facts fit
levers.saves: The base rate and the Section 301 duty: the provision below is Free
levers.appliesTo: U.S. sugar or candy that was exported and comes back unchanged (for example a rejected export shipment)
levers.document: Proof that the goods are U.S. products returned unchanged.
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duties do not apply to goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision when CBP agrees the entry is appropriate, except 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 entries (U.S. note 52(a)).

provisions.text: Products of the United States returned after export without being advanced in value or improved in condition abroad

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Claim drawback when imported sugar or syrups are exported in products
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on sugar, syrups or candy that are exported or used to make exported products
levers.appliesTo: Any line, when the imported product (or substitutable product under the same 8-digit subheading) is exported — for example over-quota sugar used in exported confectionery
levers.document: A drawback claim with import and export records linking the two.
levers.caveat: Not every extra duty is eligible for drawback; confirm with CBP before pricing on it.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty on classification — raw vs. refined, sugar syrup vs. blended syrup, sugar-containing article under notes 2–3 or retail candy — which decides whether a quota line applies
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product and the intended entry.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product may need its own.

finalConclusion.h1: HTS Chapter 17: Sugars and Sugar Confectionery — Tariff FAQ

seo.title: Sugar & Candy Tariffs FAQ: Sugar Quota, Brazil & Mexico Sugar, Maple Syrup, Candy, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 17) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about sugar and candy tariffs: the U.S. sugar quota, the tariff on Brazilian and Mexican sugar, Canadian maple syrup, Mexican and European candy, HS codes for sugar, candy and maple syrup, and how to import sugar or candy into the U.S.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing sugar, syrups and candy into the U.S. — the sugar quota, tariffs by country, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Sugar is under tariff-rate quotas: in quota, raw cane sugar pays about 1.38¢/kg (Free under CAFTA-DR and other FTAs) and no Section 301 duty; over quota it pays 33.87¢/kg (35.74¢/kg refined) plus the country's extra duty.

Candy, syrups and over-quota sugar from the 60 Section 301 economies pay an extra duty since July 24, 2026: EU 10% in total, +10% or +12.5% for most, +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying Mexican and Canadian goods — including Canadian maple syrup and Mexican candy — enter free.

Canadian lactose, glucose and fructose syrups and molasses pay 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA, and Canadian molasses is banned from September 29, 2026. FY 2027 sugar quotas: 1,117,195 t raw value of raw cane sugar and 22,000 t of refined sugar.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on imported sugar?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether the sugar enters in quota. Raw cane sugar entered against a country's allocation pays 1.4606¢/kg less 0.020668¢ per degree under 100° polarity — about 1.38¢/kg at 96° — and Free under CAFTA-DR, Colombia, Peru and other FTAs; in-quota sugar is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties. Sugar over the quota pays 33.87¢/kg raw or 35.74¢/kg refined, plus the country's Section 301 duty. USMCA-qualifying Mexican sugar is duty-free.

faqs.question: How does the U.S. sugar import quota work?
faqs.answer: Each fiscal year USDA sets the quotas — for FY 2027 (from October 1, 2026) 1,117,195 metric tons raw value of raw cane sugar and 22,000 t of refined sugar — and USTR allocates them by country: the Dominican Republic 201,274 t, the Philippines 154,386 t, Brazil 100,000 t, Australia 94,919 t, Guatemala 54,893 t and others. In-quota sugar needs a certificate of quota eligibility from the exporting country. Mexico supplies outside the WTO quota under USMCA and the suspension agreements.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Brazilian sugar?
faqs.answer: Brazil has a 100,000 t raw sugar allocation for FY 2027. In quota it pays about 1.38¢/kg plus the 25% Section 301 duty on Brazil (9903.05.01) — in-quota sugar is exempt only from the 12.5% second duty. Over quota it pays 33.87¢/kg plus 37.5% of value, more than the sugar is worth. U.S. imports of Brazilian Chapter 17 goods fell from $880M in 2024 to $316M in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on Mexican sugar?
faqs.answer: No tariff for USMCA-qualifying Mexican sugar, but how much Mexico may ship and at what minimum price are set by the agreements suspending the antidumping and countervailing duty investigations on sugar from Mexico, which Commerce continued on September 19, 2025. Mexico supplied $531M of sugar in 2025. Non-USMCA Mexican sugar would pay the over-quota rate plus 10%.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on Canadian maple syrup?
faqs.answer: No. Pure maple syrup and maple sugar (1702.20.40) are Free, USMCA-qualifying Canadian maple syrup is exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canada, and maple syrup is not on the 2026 Section 338 lists. Without a USMCA claim it would pay 10%. The U.S. imported $387M of maple syrup and sugar in 2025, almost all from Canada.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on imported candy?
faqs.answer: Most candy without cocoa (1704.90.35) pays 5.6%, chewing gum 4%, cough drops Free. Mexican and Canadian candy is Free with a USMCA claim. Since July 24, 2026 candy from the 60 Section 301 economies pays an extra duty: EU candy 10% in total, Turkish and Thai candy 5.6% + 12.5%, Chinese candy 5.6% + 37.5%. Chocolate candy is in Chapter 18.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for sugar?
faqs.answer: Cane or beet sugar is heading 1701: raw beet sugar 1701.12, non-centrifugal cane sugar such as panela 1701.13, other raw cane sugar 1701.14, flavored or colored sugar 1701.91 and refined white sugar 1701.99. Each splits into a general note 15 line, an in-quota line and an over-quota "Other" line. Brown sugar is usually 1701.99 or 1701.91.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for candy?
faqs.answer: Candy without cocoa is 1704: chewing gum 1704.10 (4%) and other sugar confectionery 1704.90 — hard candy, gummies, lollipops and marshmallows mostly under 1704.90.35 (5.6%), white chocolate under 1704.90. Candy containing cocoa or chocolate is 1806.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for maple syrup, glucose syrup and lactose?
faqs.answer: Maple syrup and maple sugar are 1702.20 (pure product 1702.20.40, Free); lactose 1702.11 and 1702.19 (6.4%); glucose and glucose syrup 1702.30 and 1702.40; fructose 1702.50 and 1702.60; invert sugar and other syrups 1702.90. Syrups blended with cane or beet sugar fall under the sugar quotas.

faqs.question: What do I need to import sugar or candy into the U.S.?
faqs.answer: Every shipment needs FDA prior notice (21 CFR 1.281) and the importer a foreign supplier verification program (21 CFR 1.502). In-quota sugar also needs a certificate of quota eligibility from the exporting country (15 CFR 2011.103); sugar for refining and re-export or polyhydric alcohols can enter under a USDA license (7 CFR part 1530). Retail candy needs country-of-origin marking.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import its sugar and candy from?
searchedAs: where does the us get sugar
faqs.answer: $6.48B of Chapter 17 goods in 2025, down 9.7%: Mexico $1.92B and Canada $1.18B (48% together), then Brazil, Türkiye, Germany, Guatemala, Colombia, China and the Dominican Republic. Raw cane sugar was $1.29B (Mexico, Brazil, Guatemala, the Dominican Republic, Colombia), candy $3.31B (Mexico, Canada) and maple syrup $387M (Canada).
